key_findings.finding: For pregestational type 1 or type 2 diabetes with poor periconception control, major congenital malformations—especially cardiovascular and genitourinary defects—are the best-fitting leading cause of perinatal mortality among the listed choices. At 8 weeks, organogenesis is ongoing, so HbA1c around 10% is particularly concerning for embryopathy; the competing risks of macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycemia are predominantly later-pregnancy/neonatal consequences, while placental insufficiency and stillbirth are later gestational complications.

source_tools.relevance: Direct early-pregnancy cohort: congenital anomalies occurred in 13.4%, major malformations in 6.3%, and early HbA1c >7% was associated with a 3–5-fold increase in major malformation rate; cardiovascular/genitourinary defects comprised 58.8% of anomalies.
Clinical review states poorly controlled preconception/first-trimester pregestational diabetes increases major congenital malformations, stillbirth, and perinatal mortality.

key_findings.finding: The congenital-anomaly risk rises approximately linearly with early-pregnancy HbA1c; published summaries report fetal malformation incidence reaching about 15% in the highest HbA1c categories and about 20% when HbA1c is ≥13%, so HbA1c near 10% represents a substantially elevated risk rather than a modest one. Exact risk at precisely 10% is not established by the retrieved evidence.

source_tools.relevance: Review of pregnancies with pregestational diabetes reports a linear relationship between HbA1c and malformations, with incidence progressively reaching 15% in the highest HbA1c categories.
Expert review reports approximately 20% congenital-malformation risk at HbA1c ≥13%, supporting marked dose-response escalation with poor early control.

key_findings.finding: Pregestational diabetes also increases stillbirth, preterm birth, excessive fetal growth/macrosomia, and neonatal hypoglycemia, but these are broad downstream adverse outcomes and do not displace congenital malformations as the most appropriate answer for an 8-week pregnancy with poor periconception glycemic control.

source_tools.relevance: Dysglycemia review lists neonatal mortality, stillbirth, preterm delivery, excessive fetal growth, and congenital abnormalities as serious diabetic-pregnancy outcomes.
Expert review specifically links diabetes in pregnancy with preterm delivery, macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycemia, and stillbirth.
